issues.subcategory: Inconsistent operationalization across behaviors
issues.description: The study uses validated, behavior-specific measures for pornography (Brief Pornography Screen) and gambling (Problem Gambling Severity Index) but relies on modified NIDA-ASSIST items for all substance use disorders. This creates a fundamental asymmetry: pornography and gambling are assessed with psychometrically validated instruments designed to capture the specific phenomenology of those problems, while substance use problems are assessed with a general screening tool. If moral incongruence effects are found for pornography but not substances, this could be an artifact of measurement sensitivity differences rather than a true difference in the moral incongruence phenomenon. The authors acknowledge including NIDA-ASSIST items for pornography and gambling as well, but the primary analyses for those behaviors use the validated scales, creating an uneven comparison.
issues.quote: In addition to the modified NIDA-ASSIST items listed above, self-reported feelings of addiction to pornography will be assessed using the Brief Pornography Screen... In addition to the modified NIDA-ASSIST items listed above, problem gambling behavior will be measured using the Problem Gambling Severity Index

issues.subcategory: Non-representative oversample biasing gambling analyses
issues.description: The gambling sample includes 1,500 sports-wagering individuals in addition to the 2,500 representative sample, yielding an effective N of 3,325 for gambling. This oversample of sports bettors will substantially skew the gambling subsample toward more frequent and potentially more engaged gamblers compared to the general population. This could inflate or deflate moral incongruence effects for gambling in ways that are not comparable to how other behaviors are assessed in the representative sample alone. The authors do not describe any plan to analyze the representative sample separately for gambling or to weight the oversample appropriately.
issues.quote: we will also recruit an additional 1,500 adults with recent (past year) history of wagering on sports generally or sporting events specifically... Gambling 73% (national sample) 100% (sports-betting oversample) 3,325

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent effect size conversions
issues.description: The authors report converting between effect size metrics (ΔR², f², Cohen's d, β) but some conversions appear inconsistent. For example, they report β=.11 corresponding to ΔR²=.012, f²=.016, Cohen's d=.25 in one place, but earlier state the SESOI as δ=.27. They also report ΔR²=.014, f²=.020, Cohen's d=.24 for one study and ΔR²=.012, f²=.016, Cohen's d=.22 for another, but then state the SESOI δ=.27 which doesn't clearly correspond to either. The relationship between β=.11 and Cohen's d=.25 is also not straightforward without knowing the specific model parameters. These inconsistencies make it difficult to evaluate whether the equivalence bounds are correctly specified.
issues.quote: we elected to set our SESOI (δ) for our equivalence interval equal to the observed standardized estimate (β value) corresponding to the smallest effect listed above (β=.11, ΔR2 = .012, f2 = .016, Cohen's d = .25, Grubbs, Lee, et al., 2020)... We will use the Anderson-Hauck equivalence test for regression (Counsell & Cribbie, 2015), with an equivalence region based on the smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) of δ= .27.

issues.subcategory: Moral disapproval construct conflation with stigma and guilt
issues.description: The single-item measure of moral disapproval ('I believe that using ________ is morally wrong') may capture different constructs across different behaviors. For substances like alcohol and illicit drugs, moral disapproval is heavily confounded with internalized stigma, health concerns, and legal concerns. For pornography, moral disapproval is more likely to reflect genuine moral/religious values. The authors do not address whether 'moral disapproval' means the same thing psychologically across these very different behavioral domains. This threatens the validity of cross-domain comparisons, which is the central purpose of the study.
issues.quote: we will include a series of single-item moral disapproval questions that match previous measures of moral disapproval of pornography. For each substance, we will ask participants to rate their agreement with the following statement 'I believe that using ________ is morally wrong'

issues.subcategory: PGSI scoring errors in supplemental materials
issues.description: The Problem Gambling Severity Index response options shown in the supplemental materials are incorrectly scored. The standard PGSI uses a 0-3 scale (Never=0, Sometimes=1, Most of the time=2, Almost always=3). The supplemental materials show Never=0, Sometimes=2, Most of the time=4, Almost Always=5, which is not the validated scoring system. This would inflate PGSI scores and alter the psychometric properties of the measure.
issues.quote: Never (0) | Sometimes (2) | Most of the time (4) | Almost Always (5)

issues.subcategory: Brief Pornography Screen scoring errors in supplemental materials
issues.description: The Brief Pornography Screen response options shown in the supplemental materials use scoring of 0, 2, 4 (Never=0, Occasionally=2, Very Often=4), whereas the validated BPS uses 0, 1, 2 scoring. The methods section states 'on a three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often)' which contradicts the supplemental materials. This discrepancy could substantially affect the psychometric properties and comparability with prior validation studies.
issues.quote: Never (0) | Occasionally (2) | Very Often (4)... on a three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often). Responses are summed.

issues.subcategory: Underpowered subgroups for key comparisons
issues.description: The study is critically underpowered for prescription drug misuse (estimated n=140, power=.301) and illicit substance use (estimated n=240-480, power=.472-.764) to detect the SESOI. This means that for two of the seven non-pornography behaviors, the study cannot adequately test the core hypotheses. The fallback plan of using a wider equivalence region based on the pornography effect's CI lower bound is a substantially weaker test that cannot distinguish between 'no moral incongruence effect' and 'a smaller but real moral incongruence effect.'
issues.quote: However, in the case of illicit drug use (prevalence estimated at 6%-12% of the population) and prescription drug misuse (prevalence estimated at 3.5% of the population), it is possible, if not probable, that our final sample sizes will fall below the minimum size required to detect effects that small

issues.subcategory: Multiple fallback analytic strategies
issues.description: The analytic plan includes multiple contingency plans that introduce researcher degrees of freedom: (1) if assumptions are violated, supplemental analyses will be conducted but OLS results presented if 'robust'; (2) if equivalence tests fail, a secondary equivalence region based on the pornography CI lower bound will be used; (3) for underpowered subgroups, yet another alternative equivalence region is proposed. The criteria for when to invoke each fallback are not precisely specified, and the definition of 'robust' (sign and significance remain the same) is vague.
issues.quote: Should results of moderation analyses remain robust (i.e., sign and significance of interaction effects remain the same across analytic techniques), we will present OLS results... In the event that, contrary to hypotheses, the effects of moral incongruence for gambling and substances exceed our region of equivalence based on our SESOI, we will conduct exploratory analyses wherein we redefine the region of equivalence

issues.subcategory: No correction for multiple comparisons across 8 models
issues.description: The study proposes 8 separate moderation analyses (one per behavior/substance) but does not describe any correction for multiple testing across these models. While Holm corrections are mentioned for bivariate correlations, no such correction is planned for the primary hypothesis tests. With 8 tests, the family-wise error rate is substantially inflated, which is particularly problematic given that the hypotheses predict a mix of significant and null effects.
issues.quote: In total, we will conduct 8 moderation analyses for moral disapproval and frequency, corresponding to the 8 target behaviors/variables of interest

issues.subcategory: Mixing frequency and severity scales across NIDA-ASSIST items
issues.description: The NIDA-ASSIST composite for problematic use averages items on fundamentally different scales: three frequency-based items scored 0-5 and two yes/no/recency items scored 0/3/6. Averaging these together without standardization creates a composite where the two recency items (with a range of 0-6) are weighted more heavily than the frequency items (range 0-5). This is not the standard ASSIST scoring procedure and has unknown psychometric properties.
issues.quote: Participants will also respond to two questions... on 3 point scale (0 = No, Never; 3 = Yes, but not in the past 3 months; and 6 = Yes, In the past 3 months). Responses to each of the above five items will be averaged for each substance of interest

issues.subcategory: Cross-sectional design limits causal claims
issues.description: The study is cross-sectional, which fundamentally limits the ability to establish that moral incongruence 'predicts' or 'contributes to' feelings of addiction. The language throughout the manuscript implies directional/causal relationships (moral incongruence predicting feelings of addiction), but the design can only establish associations. While the authors acknowledge this in limitations, the hypotheses and framing consistently use causal language.
issues.quote: This sample is cross-sectional, which limits the temporal ordering of variables... moral incongruence (the interaction of behavioral frequency and moral disapproval of a behavior) is uniquely related to sexual behavior

issues.subcategory: Absence of attention checks or validity indicators
issues.description: The authors state they do not anticipate needing to remove responses due to inattentive responding, relying entirely on YouGov's proprietary quality control. However, no specific attention checks, validity indicators, or response consistency measures are included in the survey itself. For a study with this many parallel items across behaviors, careless responding could systematically affect results, particularly by inflating cross-behavior correlations.
issues.quote: As this data will be obtained via YouGov Opinion Polling, certain measures of quality control and responsiveness are guaranteed as a part of their data collection process based on their proprietary data collection standards. Accordingly, we do not anticipate having to remove responses from the dataset due to inattentive or invalid response styles

issues.subcategory: Gambling frequency measurement oversimplification
issues.description: Gambling frequency is assessed with a single item about 'any gambling behavior' despite the enormous heterogeneity of gambling activities (casinos, lottery, sports betting, fantasy sports, etc.). Different gambling activities have very different frequencies, risk profiles, and moral valences. A person who buys a weekly lottery ticket and a person who gambles daily at a casino would be treated equivalently. The authors mention taking an average across gambling behaviors but only show one item in the supplemental materials.
issues.quote: To form a measure of gambling frequency, an average across gambling behaviors will be taken... Gambled or placed bets at all

issues.subcategory: Contradictory description of SESOI and equivalence region
issues.description: The text states the SESOI is set to δ=.27 in one location but then describes it as being set to β=.11 (the smallest observed standardized estimate). These are very different values. The equivalence region of δ=.27 appears to come from a different study/effect (β=.270 from Study 1, Sample 3 of Grubbs, Kraus, et al., 2020), not from the smallest effect. This creates confusion about what the actual equivalence bounds are.
issues.quote: We will use the Anderson-Hauck equivalence test for regression (Counsell & Cribbie, 2015), with an equivalence region based on the smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) of δ= .27... we elected to set our SESOI (δ) for our equivalence interval equal to the observed standardized estimate (β value) corresponding to the smallest effect listed above (β=.11

issues.subcategory: Missing details on how sports-betting oversample will be handled
issues.description: The 1,500 sports-betting oversample will substantially affect the composition of the total sample, particularly for gambling analyses. The authors do not specify whether analyses will be conducted on the full combined sample, the representative sample only, or both. They do not describe any weighting procedures to account for the oversample. This is critical because the oversample could bias results for gambling (and potentially other behaviors if sports bettors differ systematically on other substance use patterns).
issues.quote: Due to the design of the larger project from which this sample is taken, we will also recruit an additional 1,500 adults with recent (past year) history of wagering on sports generally or sporting events specifically. This will provide us with a total sample of over 4,000 American adults.

issues.subcategory: Confirmatory bias in hypothesis framing
issues.description: The authors explicitly state they aim to demonstrate that moral incongruence is unique to sexual behavior ('with a specific goal of demonstrating that moral incongruence is unique in predicting compulsive sexual behaviors'). This framing suggests confirmatory rather than exploratory intent, which is concerning given that the theoretical basis for why moral incongruence should be unique to sexual behavior (vs. other morally laden behaviors) is not well articulated. The authors acknowledge that moral disapproval exists for gambling and substance use but do not provide a clear theoretical mechanism for why the interaction effect should be absent for these behaviors.
issues.quote: with a specific goal of demonstrating that moral incongruence is unique in predicting compulsive sexual behaviors

issues.subcategory: Temporal mismatch between frequency and outcome measures
issues.description: Frequency measures assess past 12-month behavior, the NIDA-ASSIST problematic use items assess past 3 months, and the Brief Pornography Screen assesses the past 6 months. These temporal mismatches mean that the interaction of 12-month frequency with moral disapproval is being used to predict problems assessed over different, shorter time windows. Someone whose behavior changed substantially over the year could show misleading patterns.
issues.quote: participants will report the frequency with which they have engaged in those behaviors over the past 12 months... In the past three months, how often have you had a strong desire or urge... In the last 6 months, have any of these situations happened to you

issues.subcategory: Floor effects in outcome measures for low-prevalence behaviors
issues.description: For behaviors with low prevalence (prescription drug misuse, illicit drugs), the outcome measures are likely to show extreme floor effects, with the vast majority of users reporting no or minimal problems. This severely restricts variance in the dependent variable and makes it very difficult to detect interaction effects, independent of sample size concerns. The authors do not discuss this issue or plan for it analytically.
issues.quote: Prescription Drug Misuse 3.5% 140... Illicit Substances 6%-12% 240-480

issues.subcategory: Gender operationalization unclear
issues.description: Gender is described as 'binary where 1 = male, and 0 = not-male' for the moderation analyses, but the YouGov panel data likely includes more nuanced gender categories. The authors do not describe how non-binary or other gender identities will be handled, nor do they justify the binary coding decision. This is particularly relevant given that gender is included as a covariate in all models.
issues.quote: gender (binary where 1 = male, and 0 =not-male)

issues.subcategory: No validated measures for substance-specific problematic use
issues.description: While pornography and gambling have validated, behavior-specific outcome measures (BPS and PGSI), no validated substance-specific measures are included (e.g., AUDIT for alcohol, FTND for nicotine, CUDIT for cannabis). The modified NIDA-ASSIST items used for substances have not been validated as outcome measures in the way they are being used here. This asymmetry in measurement quality across behaviors is a fundamental threat to the study's ability to make valid cross-behavior comparisons.
issues.quote: Alcohol: Average of modified NIDA-ASSIST items for specific substances... Tobacco/Nicotine products: Average of modified NIDA-ASSIST items for specific substances

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent frequency scale description
issues.description: The frequency scale is described as ranging from '1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day)' in the pornography section but shown as '0 (never) to 5 (more than once per day)' in the substance use section and supplemental materials. This inconsistency appears in multiple places and creates confusion about the actual coding scheme.
issues.quote: Pornography viewing frequency will be assessed using the same modified frequency scale as is present on the ASSIST, wherein participants will report past-year frequency of pornography use on a scale of 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day)... participants will report the frequency with which they have engaged in those behaviors over the past 12 months on a scale of 0 (never) to 5 (more than once per day)

issues.subcategory: BPS item 5 confounds moral incongruence with outcome
issues.description: Item 5 of the Brief Pornography Screen ('You continue to use pornography even though you feel guilty about it') directly taps into guilt about pornography use, which is conceptually overlapping with moral incongruence. Including this item in the outcome measure when moral disapproval is a predictor creates criterion contamination—the predictor and outcome share conceptual and likely empirical variance, potentially inflating the moral incongruence effect specifically for pornography relative to other behaviors whose outcome measures don't contain guilt items.
issues.quote: 5. You continue to use pornography even though you feel guilty about it.

issues.subcategory: Missing plan for handling non-users on moral disapproval
issues.description: The authors state that measures of problematic use and moral disapproval will be administered to all participants regardless of engagement. However, the analytic plan only describes analyzing users of each behavior. It is unclear how moral disapproval ratings from non-users will be handled—will they be excluded from analyses? If so, this creates a selection effect where only people who engage in a behavior despite disapproving of it are included, which is the very phenomenon being studied.
issues.quote: we will administer measures of problematic use and moral disapproval to all participants in the sample. Therefore, for each analysis, we anticipate having slightly different subsets of the total sample.

issues.subcategory: Asymmetric base rates of moral disapproval across behaviors
issues.description: The base rates of moral disapproval likely vary enormously across behaviors. Most people do not morally disapprove of alcohol use, while many morally disapprove of illicit drug use or pornography. This means the distribution of the moral disapproval variable and the nature of the interaction will be fundamentally different across behaviors. A null interaction for alcohol might simply reflect insufficient variance in moral disapproval rather than a true absence of the moral incongruence effect. The authors do not discuss this critical issue or plan sensitivity analyses to address it.
issues.quote: For each substance, we will ask participants to rate their agreement with the following statement 'I believe that using ________ is morally wrong'

issues.subcategory: Dual outcome measures for pornography and gambling without clear primary specification
issues.description: For pornography and gambling, both validated scales (BPS, PGSI) and modified NIDA-ASSIST items will be collected. The text mentions 8 moderation analyses but Table 1 shows both measures for pornography and gambling. It is not entirely clear which outcome is the primary test for each hypothesis, creating potential for selective reporting of whichever outcome better supports the hypotheses.
issues.quote: Pornography Use: Brief Pornography Screen Sum Score and modified NIDA-ASSIST items... Gambling Behavior: Problem Gambling Severity Index and modified NIDA-ASSIST items

issues.subcategory: Religiousness measured differently than in prior studies
issues.description: The religiousness measure uses three Pew Research Center items about religious importance, prayer, and attendance, averaged after standardization and sign-reversed. Prior studies that established the moral incongruence effect used different religiousness measures. The comparability of this operationalization with prior work is not established, which matters because the authors are trying to replicate and extend prior findings.
issues.quote: Religiousness will be measured via the average of standardized responses to three items taken from Pew Research Center... upon taking the average of standardized responses to the above three questions, the average will be transformed by multiplying by -1 so that higher scores correspond to higher religiousness.

issues.subcategory: Mismatch between introduction and analytic plan on moral incongruence definition
issues.description: The introduction describes moral incongruence as 'the interaction of moral disapproval of a behavior and the frequency of engaging in that behavior,' but the analytic plan later mentions 'the interaction of moral disapproval of an action with severity of consequences from the action.' These are different constructs—frequency of behavior vs. severity of consequences—and the inconsistency suggests confusion about the operationalization.
issues.quote: Central to the proposed study is the measurement of moral incongruence as the interaction of moral disapproval of an action with severity of consequences from the action.

issues.subcategory: U.S.-only sample limits cross-cultural generalizability
issues.description: The study uses only a U.S. sample, but moral attitudes toward sexual behavior, gambling, and substance use vary enormously across cultures. The authors acknowledge this briefly in limitations but frame their hypotheses and conclusions in universal terms about the nature of moral incongruence and addiction. Given that prior work has shown cultural variation in moral incongruence effects, findings may not generalize beyond the U.S. context.
issues.quote: Although a nationally representative sample in the U.S. is better than convenience sampling methods, such a sample represents only one broad cultural context in which these hypotheses could be tested.

issues.subcategory: No plan for handling missing data
issues.description: The authors state they 'anticipate no unplanned missingness of data' based on YouGov's data collection standards. This is unrealistic for a survey of this length and complexity, particularly given that different subsets of items are administered based on endorsement of past-year use. No plan for handling missing data (e.g., multiple imputation, FIML) is described, nor are criteria specified for what level of missingness would trigger concern.
issues.quote: Additionally, we anticipate no unplanned missingness of data.
